Current international law can regulate AWS responsibly while allowing strategic use.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.69790/epis-rep-aic-1/39949\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 10, 15]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6238401\", \"title\": [\"Registering the Machine: A Framework for Autonomous Agent Accountability\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><p>Autonomous AI agents represent a regulatory inflection point comparable to the introduction of motor vehicles, aircraft, or securities markets—each of which eventually required a registration system.&nbsp;&nbsp;<span>They exhibit characteristics that distinguish them from traditional software: persistence, autonomy, and goal-directedness. They operate continuously, make decisions without human approval at each step, and adapt their behavior based on environmental feedback. As these agents increasingly manage portfolios, negotiate contracts, provide medical guidance, and control physical systems, existing legal frameworks—including products liability, agency law, and platform intermediary doctrines—fail to establish clear accountability when harm occurs.</span></p>\\n<p>This Article proposes a three-pillar registration framework for autonomous agents, drawing on the technical architecture of ERC-8004 (\\\"Trustless Agents\\\") and lessons from securities regulation, aviation oversight, and motor vehicle registration. The framework consists of: (1) an&nbsp;<span>Identity Registry</span>&nbsp;providing unique, persistent identifiers linked to responsible legal persons; (2) a&nbsp;<span>Reputation Registry</span>&nbsp;collecting performance and compliance information; and (3) a&nbsp;<span>Validation Registry</span>&nbsp;certifying compliance with baseline safety standards. The Article addresses implementation challenges including federal-state allocation of authority, self-regulatory organization design, international coordination, capability-based thresholds, enforcement mechanisms, and phased deployment.</p>\\n<p>The Article responds to four principal objections: that registration will chill innovation, that the technical infrastructure is infeasible, that constitutional constraints prohibit compelled disclosure, and that jurisdictional arbitrage will render domestic regulation ineffective. Each objection has force, but none is fatal. Registration, properly understood, is not bureaucratic overhead—it is a time-tested mechanism for producing information that enables accountability, adapted across centuries and across domains. The window for proactive regulation is narrowing.</p></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6238401\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.5771/9783748909538-121\", \"title\": [\"Chapter III  The “Accountability Gap” Problem.
